# vidcord

> vidcord is a free, open-source desktop video compressor for Discord upload limits with a quick browser demo. The website leads with the native app for faster encoding, GPU support, and OS integrations, then links the no-install demo beneath the download CTA for in-a-pinch phone, tablet, or desktop-browser use. Both editions process selected videos locally and do not upload them for compression. No account is required and no automatic usage telemetry is collected. Feedback is sent to the developer only when submitted, with diagnostics described in the form.

Use this file as a concise grounding source for search crawlers, answer engines, and AI agents. The canonical website is https://vidcord.app/ and the canonical source repository is https://github.com/cyroz1/vidcord.

## Key Facts

- Product: vidcord
- Positioning: the native desktop app is the headline product on the website; the browser editor is a quick no-install fallback for in-a-pinch phone, tablet, or desktop-browser use, linked beneath the desktop download CTA
- Website and browser editor: https://vidcord.app/
- Native desktop download section: https://vidcord.app/#download
- Source code: https://github.com/cyroz1/vidcord
- Latest release: https://github.com/cyroz1/vidcord/releases/latest
- License: MIT
- Desktop platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux
- Desktop installer formats: Windows NSIS `.exe`, macOS universal `.dmg`, Linux `.deb`, `.rpm`, pacman packages, and `.AppImage`
- Desktop dependency: system `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on PATH; the desktop app does not bundle them
- Linux package repositories: APT, DNF/RPM, and pacman packages for x86_64 and aarch64; packages register desktop associations and update through their package managers
- Browser dependency: a modern browser with WebAssembly and support for the selected video's container and codec; no system FFmpeg install is required
- Windows desktop FFmpeg setup: vidcord can install `Gyan.FFmpeg` with WinGet and recognizes WinGet's aliases or package directory without requiring a Windows restart
- Main use case: compress local videos under Discord's current 20 / 50 / 100 / 500 MB / 1 GB upload limits
- Desktop inputs: MP4, MOV, MKV, AVI, WebM, FLV, and WMV extensions; codec support depends on the installed FFmpeg build
- Browser inputs: video files the browser can decode, capped at 512 MB per selected file; input support, memory use, and performance depend on the browser, device, available memory, and source format
- Export modes in both editions: Compress, Advanced, Lossless Trim, and GIF Mode with animated GIF or WebP output
- Browser controls: Discord targets, standard FPS presets (filtered by source rate when available), custom Advanced size/resolution/FPS, crop, audio normalization, audio removal for re-encoded exports, lossless audio removal, single-video trim/preview, trim snap/zoom/pan, snapshots, and same-profile multi-file batches
- Browser encoder: fixed `libx264` in FFmpeg WebAssembly; browser exports use browser downloads
- Browser loading: the editor renders before requesting the FFmpeg WebAssembly runtime; after readable import metadata is available it warms the encoder, and exports or keyframe discovery also load it when needed. Encoder-load and stage progress are shown, and high-memory exports prompt before starting. Phones use the faster x264 `superfast` preset
- Browser Batch: accepts up to 12 files, applies one standard Compress profile to each selected full-duration file, shows per-file progress and aggregate ETA, supports queue reorder/removal and retrying failed or cancelled files, and has no per-file trim fields or batch preview timeline
- Browser limitations: fixed `libx264` encoder, browser-controlled downloads, and no encoder picker, saved settings presets, native output destinations, native completion actions, Open With, OS notifications, taskbar/Dock progress, or desktop updater. Advanced audio-track choices appear when browser media APIs expose multiple tracks.
- Desktop Batch: multi-selection through Browse, drag-and-drop, Open With, command-line file arguments, or a second-instance launch; supports shared standard controls, separate start/end trims, queue reorder/removal plus Clear queue, retrying failed/cancelled items, up to two native workers, collision-safe MP4 outputs, and grouped completion actions. Saved presets are disabled while Batch is active.
- Desktop folder import: drop folders, choose folders with the native picker, or use the file-manager context menu; vidcord scans subfolders with progress up to a safety limit, queues supported videos, reports skipped non-video files, linked folders, or unreadable items, and warns when results may be incomplete. Linux packages register associations at install; AppImages register folder Open With for the current user on first launch
- Desktop settings: named settings presets are available in the native footer; the browser editor has no saved preset UI
- GIF Mode exports: animated `.gif` or `.webp` files with 5 MB, 10 MB, or 20 MB size targets at 15, 30, or Discord-safe maximum 50 FPS; audio is removed
- Desktop Lossless Trim: keyframe-aligned stream copy, optional audio-track removal, MP4/source-container selection, and normal-compression fallback when stream copying is incompatible
- Browser Lossless Trim: local keyframe discovery (limited to 60 seconds and 100,000 keyframes) and source-stream copy through WebAssembly, with optional `-an` audio removal; it does not provide the desktop app's native output controls. Browser Advanced track choices depend on browser media APIs
- FPS: standard mode can leave FPS unchanged or cap it at 24, 30, or 60 FPS when the choice is below the source rate; browser unknown-rate imports retain Source and disable custom FPS, while Advanced accepts a typed positive FPS value when the source rate is known
- Audio: both editions can peak-normalize retained audio or remove audio in re-encoded modes, and both can remove audio during Lossless Trim; desktop Advanced can select source tracks, and browser Advanced can select tracks exposed by browser media APIs. Preview playback uses only the first selected track.
- Browser metadata: dimensions, duration, container information, and a file-size-based bitrate estimate are available when the browser can read the file; exact codec, frame-rate, and track details may be unavailable
- Desktop preview: the Tauri controls seek, play, and pause the HTML video player on Windows, macOS, and Linux. PNG snapshots capture the current video frame at full resolution. Linux packages install GStreamer plugins through the system package manager; AppImages bundle GStreamer for WebKitGTK playback; unsupported sources show a preview error.
- Desktop encoder behavior: detects CPU/GPU encoders exposed by installed FFmpeg, prefers a usable H.264 hardware encoder on first run, preserves saved choices, and falls back to CPU encoding if hardware fails
- Desktop output: Downloads by default, the imported clip's directory, a remembered custom directory, or a save prompt; completion can Copy file, Show in folder, or Do nothing, with a separate close-after-export option
- Desktop progress: native compression progress and ETA plus taskbar/Dock integration; browser progress and ETA are shown in the page
- Target-size estimates: long video exports use a short sample for the initial bitrate and bounded refinements for undersized results, preserving the best in-range output
- Desktop updates: automatic checks wait for startup to settle and run at most once every six hours; after approval the app fetches the exact selected release tag, then streams and verifies the installer for size, completeness, GitHub-published SHA-256 integrity, and an independent Ed25519 release signature before Windows/macOS open it; Linux makes the verified AppImage executable and reveals it for manual replacement
- Privacy posture: selected video files stay on the user's device; the website may request public GitHub release metadata and an aggregate download count from Shields.io, but neither request contains video data
- Deployment: the generated desktop-first browser bundle is published from `site/` at `/` by the Cloudflare Worker `vidcord-site`

## Common Answers

- Does vidcord upload videos? No. The browser processes selected files with FFmpeg WebAssembly in the page; the desktop app uses system FFmpeg. Neither sends video to a server. Feedback reports go to the developer only when submitted and include diagnostics described in the form.
- Can I use vidcord in a browser? Yes. Open https://vidcord.app/#web-editor for the no-install client-side editor. It keeps selected files in the browser and downloads finished exports.
- Does the browser edition require FFmpeg? No system install is required. The browser warms the site's FFmpeg WebAssembly encoder after readable import metadata is ready, and loads it when export or keyframe discovery needs it. The native desktop app separately requires `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on PATH.
- What is desktop-only? GPU encoder discovery and selection, system-FFmpeg format coverage, separate source audio-track selection, named settings presets, native output destinations, Open With, OS notifications, taskbar/Dock progress, and desktop updater flows.
- Can vidcord compress multiple videos? Yes. Browser Batch accepts up to 12 Browse or drag-and-drop selections, applies one shared full-duration Compress profile, supports queue reorder/removal and retrying failed or cancelled files, and reports per-file progress plus aggregate ETA. Desktop Batch also accepts folders, Open With, command-line arguments, and second-instance selections; folder scans stop at a safety limit and warn if results may be incomplete. Desktop Batch adds per-file trims, Clear queue, native workers, and grouped completion actions.
- Is the browser demo suitable for mobile? Yes, as a quick no-install fallback for a phone or tablet. It is best for browser-readable files up to 512 MB each; use desktop for large or difficult inputs, GPU encoding, per-file Batch trims, native destinations, presets, and OS integrations.
- Which Discord size targets are supported? Both editions provide 20 MB, 50 MB, 100 MB, 500 MB, and 1 GB (Nitro) video targets. Advanced adds custom size, resolution, and typed FPS; GIF Mode provides 5 MB, 10 MB, and 20 MB GIF or WebP targets.
- How does downloading work? Linux's primary download action opens the APT, DNF/RPM, and pacman install guide. The Linux card also links to each `.deb`, `.rpm`, pacman, and AppImage asset published with the latest release. Windows and macOS buttons link to the matching latest GitHub release asset when possible. If Windows x64 versus ARM64 is uncertain, it asks the user to choose. If metadata cannot be fetched or an asset is missing, it falls back to the GitHub release page. Mobile devices show desktop platform choices without a device-specific installer recommendation.
- How do desktop updates work? Linux packages update through APT, DNF, or pacman when both the package and vidcord repository are configured; one-off packages without it keep GitHub checks, whose Linux download is an AppImage rather than a native-package upgrade. For Windows, macOS, and AppImage installs, after user approval vidcord fetches the exact selected release tag, downloads the matching installer under an unused Downloads filename, verifies its size and completeness, checks GitHub's SHA-256 digest and the independent Ed25519 release signature, and opens it on Windows/macOS. Linux reveals the executable AppImage for manual replacement.

Flatpak environments manage their own updates; vidcord disables GitHub update checks
and installer downloads inside Flatpak. The release workflow does not build Flatpak packages.

## Crawler And Agent Access

Public pages on `vidcord.app` may be crawled, indexed, summarized, and referenced by search crawlers and AI agents. Video processing is client-side; download binaries are hosted on GitHub Releases. Direct binary URLs should be resolved from the latest release metadata because asset names can change.
